title: Common Code Smells
summary: The local symptoms in code that predict future pain — long methods, duplicate code, feature envy, primitive obsession — catalogued the way refactoring literature does.

slides.markdown:
A **code smell** isn't a bug — the code runs fine today. It's a surface signal that something underneath will cost you later: a bug, a slow change, a confused reviewer. Think of it like a check-engine light: the car still drives, but ignoring it compounds the eventual repair.

This topic catalogs the smells you'll actually recognize in code review and interviews — long methods, duplicate code, feature envy, primitive obsession — and, just as important, when chasing them does more harm than good.

slides.sectionTitle: What a code smell actually is
slides.markdown:
A smell is a **heuristic**, not a defect report. The term comes from Kent Beck and Martin Fowler's refactoring work: code that passes every test and satisfies every requirement can still smell, because the smell is about the *cost of the next change*, not correctness right now.

A 300-line method that computes the right answer every time is not "wrong" — but if changing one branch of it takes two hours of careful reading to avoid breaking three other branches, that's the smell talking. The fix isn't always immediate; the point is to notice the signal and decide deliberately whether to act on it.

slides.sectionTitle: Long method and long parameter list
slides.markdown:
A **long method** forces a reader to hold many local variables and branches in working memory at once — past roughly 40-50 lines, most people start losing track of which flag affects which branch, and that's exactly where off-by-one and stale-state bugs hide.

A **long parameter list** has the same root cause at the call site: `createUser(name, email, true, false, null, 3)` tells you nothing about what `true` or `3` mean, so every caller either guesses or goes reading the signature. Both smells correlate with bugs for the same reason — they overload the reader's short-term memory instead of the type system.

The fix for both is usually the same move: extract a smaller method, or bundle related parameters into an object.

slides.sectionTitle: Large Class (God Class) — a smell, not yet an anti-pattern
slides.markdown:
A **Large Class** (or God Class) is a class that has quietly accumulated too many fields and methods — often because every new feature found it easiest to add "just one more method" to an already-central class. You'll spot it by the class doing unrelated things: an `Order` class that also formats invoices, sends emails, and validates tax IDs.

This is a **local, class-level smell** — noticed by reading one file. It's the seed of the **God Object anti-pattern** in [Common Design Anti-Patterns](common-design-anti-patterns), which is the architecture-level consequence once that one class becomes a dependency half the codebase routes through. Catching the smell early is how you avoid ever getting there.

slides.sectionTitle: Duplicate code and the shotgun surgery it causes
slides.markdown:
**Duplicate code** means the same logic — a discount calculation, a validation rule — is copy-pasted in multiple places instead of living in one. It looks harmless when it's written; the pain shows up later, when the business rule changes and you have to remember every copy exists.

Miss one copy and you get **shotgun surgery**: a single conceptual change ("tax now applies to shipping too") requires small edits scattered across many files, and it's easy to fix four of the five places and ship an inconsistency that only shows up in production.

The fix is the classic **Extract Method**, covered in [Refactoring to Fix Smells](refactoring-to-fix-smells) — pull the duplicated logic into one place every caller shares.

**Shotgun surgery** is what duplicate code looks like from the outside: one idea, scattered edits. The fewer places a rule lives, the fewer places you can forget to update it.

If a single-line requirement change routinely means opening five files, that's the smell asking you to consolidate the logic into one.

slides.sectionTitle: Feature envy: a method more interested in another class's data
slides.markdown:
A method has **feature envy** when it calls another object's getters over and over to do its work, instead of using the data already available on its own class. A `PricingService.applyDiscount(order)` method that calls `order.getItems()`, `order.getCustomer().getTier()`, and `order.getCustomer().getJoinDate()` five different times is spending more effort reading `Order` than doing anything `PricingService`-specific.

That's the signal that the logic is **envious of `Order`'s data** and probably belongs as a method on `Order` (or on a small object built from it) instead. Move the method to the class whose data it actually uses, and the getter-chasing disappears along with most of the coupling.

**Primitive obsession** is reaching for a `String`, `int`, or `boolean` to represent a concept that deserves its own type — an email as a bare `String` with no validation, a price as a raw `int` with no currency attached.

A **data clump** is the multi-parameter version: a group of primitives that always travel together — `street, city, zip` showing up as three separate parameters in five different method signatures. The diagnostic question is simple: *do these values always appear together, and would passing only two of them ever make sense?* If not, they're really one type that hasn't been named yet.

Naming it — an `Address`, a `Money`, an `EmailAddress` — moves validation and formatting into one place instead of re-deriving it at every call site.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: refactoring a data clump into an Address value object

slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I spotted a smell, so I should refactor it right now, in the same change as my feature."

**Why it's wrong:** refactoring is only safe when you can verify behavior didn't change, and that verification comes from tests. Restructuring a smelly method with no test around it means you're relying on manual inspection to prove nothing broke — which is exactly the kind of mistake smells are trying to help you avoid, applied to the refactor itself.

**Correct model:** treat smell-hunting as triage, not an obligation to fix immediately. If the method you need to touch has no tests, write a characterization test first (see [Refactoring to Fix Smells](refactoring-to-fix-smells)), *then* refactor — and keep the refactor in its own commit, separate from the feature change, so a regression is easy to isolate.
